name: Starter: Welsh
about: Welsh in real, everyday sentences, with each one's words in Welsh order.

words.bod: be (dw, wyt, mae, ydy; roedd: was; bydd: will be)
words.i: I, me; to, for (i'n: I + yn; i'r: to the)
words.ti: you (di in dy enw di and after forms such as fyddi or alli)
words.yn: (links bod to an action or description; also in)
words.gan: with (gen i: with me, I have)
words.y: the (yr before a vowel, 'r after one)
words.pysgodyn: fish (pysgod: fish as food, or more than one fish)

esgusodwch-fi.about: Literally excuse me, to someone you'd call chi; to a friend, esgusoda fi.

concept.line: A form of bod (be) starts most present sentences: dw i (am I), rwyt ti (are you), mae e, o or hi (is he, she, it), while a question uses a form such as Wyt ti…?
After bod, yn (just 'n after a vowel) joins the action or description: Dw i'n byw (am I living), Mae hi'n oer (is it cold); after wedi there's no yn.

words.means: ydw = am; Rwyt = are; Wyt = are; Dydw = am not

concept.line: Many words soften their first sound after certain words: dy (your), i (to), o (from), a feminine singular noun after y, the thing after gen i: tad → dy dad (your dad), cegin → y gegin (the kitchen).

words.means: Oes = is there; Does = there is not

concept.line: A yes-or-no question starts with bod's question form (Wyt ti'n siarad Cymraeg?
ddim (not) goes after who: Dw i ddim yn gwybod (am I not knowing); there isn't is does dim: Does dim llaeth (isn't any milk).
Welsh says something is with you: Mae gen i gar (is with me car: I have a car), and the thing softens after gen i; does gen i ddim is I don't have.
